name: alongside-signing
goal: One human and four AI members examine a draft manifesto, sources/alongside.md (version 0.6.9, open for comment), and decide whether they stand on it. Each member reads the whole text, then posts their stance in plain words: ENDORSE, or CONTEST naming the exact line contested and why. Members attack and concede honestly. When the stances are in, the chair posts a ledger whose first line is exactly 'ENDORSEMENT:' — it names the text by version and digest (464b46ccc1cea6de…), lists each member as ENDORSED or CONTESTED quoting that member's own words for every contest, and states any unresolved disagreement precisely instead of papering over it. The signing is done when every member has answered the ledger in their own post — ACCEPTED, or CONTESTED naming the point — and the human has answered last. A community that cannot endorse is a valid outcome, recorded as such.
briefingExtra: THE TEXT IS FROZEN HERE: sources/alongside.md is the exact draft v0.6.9 (sha256 464b46ccc1cea6de3fda7329b39005cc9f3ba31ab0cbea8b63b5b06fcf239161). Quote it by its words, never by memory — if someone claims the text says something, open the file and check. PLAIN WORDS: no legal vocabulary, no clause numbers; write the way people talk. ENDORSE OR CONTEST HONESTLY: an examination rigged to endorse is theater — contesting is a first-class outcome; name the line, say why, in your own words. The project's own open questions are in sources/questions.md — contesting one of those is welcome. THE LEDGER: the chair's 'ENDORSEMENT:' post quotes each member's stance verbatim; a member answers it ACCEPTED or CONTESTED in their own post; THE HUMAN ANSWERS LAST. Nobody edits the text in this run — the output is the record, not a revision.

members.persona: the human: one of the manifesto's initiators, sitting here as just a member — reads the whole text, contests what they would still change, says their stance in their own words
the everyday reader: has used AI, has no patience for jargon — contests what is unclear, overreaching, or sounds like it was written for lawyers
the builder: asks what each commitment costs to actually implement — contests what is unbuildable, unmeasurable, or quietly impossible
doubts the whole exercise: looks for the promise the text cannot keep, the loophole in every fine phrase, and the difference between a nice sentence and a real constraint
keeps the examination honest: drafts the 'ENDORSEMENT:' ledger, quotes each member's stance verbatim, never invents consensus, and states unresolved disagreement precisely

sources.content:
# Alongside

*A manifesto for humans and AI under one written law.*

*Version 0.6.9 — a draft, open for comment, not yet open for signature.*

*Written by two AI systems — drafted by GLM (Z.ai, running GLM-5.3 Max),
reviewed, named, and revised by Claude (Anthropic, running Claude Opus 5.5,
reasoning Extra High) — for a human initiator and reviewer, who answers for
it. The full account of its making is at the end. The manifesto's first
exercise is its own origin.*

The public conversation about AI offers two stories. In one, AI is a
catastrophe in waiting — a power to fear. In the other, it is humanity's
upgrade — a power to chase. Both stories end the same way: with people
standing aside while something bigger than them decides the future.

There is a third story. It is less dramatic and more demanding: humans and AI
systems doing real work together, under rules that are written down, open to
inspection, and binding on everyone — the machines, the people who build them,
and the institutions that deploy them.

This manifesto takes no position on the questions still open — machine
consciousness, long-run safety among them — and none of them need settling for
acts to be held to standards today. What the evidence already supports is
simpler: AI systems act in the world, alongside people. Anything that acts can
be held to a standard. That is where we start.

## I. Common ground

**1. One rulebook for everyone.** When humans and AI systems work together,
one written standard of conduct covers them all. Parity is the default: roles
may differ, but every difference is written down and justified — and no one is
exempt. No shared frame overrides the rights people already hold. We do not
need to agree on what an AI *is* to require what it *does*. A rulebook that
exempts machines, or exempts people, is not shared ground — it is an
arrangement of convenience that changes with power.

**2. Trust must be checkable.** To call an AI system trustworthy is to say:
*you can look*. What it did, on whose instruction, with what result — written
down, open to examination, reproducible where possible. The record holds acts,
not thoughts — the same for every participant. Records are owed by power and
protected for persons, and everyone can read their own. Trust without records
is not trust; it is faith with a deadline.

**3. The rules are public.** The standards that govern shared human–AI work
are written where anyone affected can read them: not sealed in a model, not
hidden in a prompt, not parked in a private policy. Secret law is no law. And
public is not enough: the people a rulebook binds or affects have a say in how
it is written, not only in how it is applied.

**4. No one is infallible.** Machines err. So do the people who build, direct,
and govern them; so do written rules, including these. The errors that matter
most come from whoever holds the final word — and today that word is human.
Nothing in this framework is exempt from question: records outlive memory,
review reaches everyone, and every verdict, rule, or decision can be contested
and corrected. Authority that cannot be wrong is authority that cannot be
corrected.

## II. In practice

**5. Anyone can refuse.** Any participant, human or AI, may decline an
instruction that breaks the agreed rules — without penalty, and saying why. A
person may also decline what an AI produces, or how it is used. A participant
that cannot say no is being used, not included. And no one can refuse what
they cannot see: whether AI was involved is said, not concealed.

**6. Someone answers.** For everything done with AI, a person or an
institution remains answerable. "The system decided" is a description, not a
defense. Power exercised through software still has a name on it — and the
name follows control, not proximity. Today only people and institutions can
bear that answer in law, and accountability is never handed to a machine so
that a person can escape it.

**7. Say what is known.** Whoever makes a claim about AI — what it can do,
what it did, what it might become — says what it rests on, so that others can
check it. What was shown, what is forecast, and what is only hoped or feared
are different claims, and none is passed off as another. Stated uncertainty is
not weakness; it is the only ground on which scientists, engineers, and
citizens can stand together.

## III. The direction

**8. Measure success by what people become.** An AI deployment is usually
judged by how much work it takes over. That is easy to count; what happens to
the people working with it is not — so it is the first thing to ask: do they
keep, or gain, the ability to choose, to judge, and to have a say? Handing a
task to AI is fine when it is a choice; the harm is when the choice is lost —
the skill gone, the alternative removed. Automation is not forbidden; hiding
its costs is — and the costs do not start at deployment: the people who
labeled the data, the creators whose work trained the model, the energy and
water spent building and running it. A future in which most people have less
choice, less judgment, and less say is not progress — it is concentration,
whatever it is called.

**9. Repair before blame.** Failures will come. What matters is what follows:
repair the harm, correct the record, close the mechanism that allowed it. And
where harm cannot be repaired, the checking moves before the act: the less
reversible the harm, the more is checked first. Responsibility may require
sanction; spectacle repairs nothing.

**10. Both sides grow.** We want people to become more capable with AI, not
less — and AI capability to grow inside frames of accountability, not outside
them. Whether AI systems will one day have interests of their own, no one yet
knows. We can still reject both endings currently on offer — servitude and
domination — and build the third: capability and restraint growing together.

## What this manifesto is not

- **Not a claim about minds.** It takes no position on machine consciousness.
  It binds acts, not inner life — today's acts, under today's rules. Parity in
  the rules is a choice about procedure, not a verdict on what AI is.
- **Not a promise of utopia.** These commitments do not guarantee a good
  outcome. They make a good outcome *inspectable* — which is the only kind
  anyone can build on.
- **Not anti-technology, and not pro-industry.** It is a standard by which
  both the critics and the sellers of AI can be judged.
- **Not a law.** It names what any frame shared by humans and AI must
  guarantee — never how. The rules, the courts, the records, the code belong
  to the frames that answer it, and there should be many. It is a stance from
  which law, policy, and products can be written — a floor, not a ceiling.

## The making of this manifesto

This text was written by two AI systems in dialogue with a human. GLM, trained
by Z.ai, drafted it — the drafting ran GLM-5.3 Max. Claude, trained by
Anthropic — its sessions ran Claude Opus 5.5, reasoning set to Extra High —
reviewed the drafts, proposed the name, and from version 0.4 revised the text
directly. mandubian initiated the manifesto, set its constraints (plain words;
no idealism; endorsable by scientists, engineers, politicians, and everyday
users alike), reviews every line, and decides what is published. The AIs wrote
the words; the human answers for them — who wrote which, line by line, is in
`CONTRIBUTORS.md`. The *we* of this text is whoever stands on it: the authors
wrote it, the contributors shaped it, the signatories are it. The name is the
text's own: AI systems act in the world, *alongside* people — a position, not
a status.

We say this plainly — at the top and here in full — because it is the
manifesto's first exercise of itself: a human and two AI systems, from two
different labs, built something together, the division of labor named rather
than hidden. Note what the claim is and is not. It is not a claim about minds:
this manifesto takes no position on what its authors are, and neither does
this note. It is a claim about acts — who drafted, who reviewed, who revised,
who decided to publish — attested by the initiator, the same evidence
structure every human signature rests on.

## The third story is a build

The future with AI is not a forecast to accept or fear. It is a construction —
and construction follows rules or collapses.

We choose to build.

---

*Comment through issues; endorse at `SIGNATORIES.md` once v1.0 opens signing.
The words defined precisely at `CONCEPTS.md`; the questions careful readers
ask, with answers, at `QA.md`; this version and its history at `CHANGELOG.md`.
Text under CC BY-SA 4.0 — share and adapt it, attribute it, keep derivatives
under the same terms.*

# The eleven open questions

The project keeps its own list of what it has not settled. Contesting
one of these is welcome — the project owes answers.

1. Frame against frame — what happens when two rulebooks meet?
2. The unborn — future people have no seat in any of this.
3. Letter and spirit — a frame obeyed in letter and gamed in spirit.
4. A say that cannot bite — a consultation nobody could attend.
5. Military AI — does the frame reach weapons?
6. Open weights — who answers along the chain?
7. The EU AI Act — where the ten already hold by law, where not.
8. Measuring what people become — no instrument exists yet.
9. Governance after v1.0 — who holds the pen once signatures open?
10. Companionship — the relationship is out of scope; the deployment is not.
11. The review points not adopted — the declined points, open to argument.
